
#  **Netflix User Engagement Analysis**
  
  
## 1,2. Data Acquisition & Recreating the Columns


For Data acquisition from the Netflix server, below script can be executed to load the data *from 2023 to 1st half of 2026* with 7 CSV files, in the local environment with a more personalized approach to benefit the **Data manipulation and EDA**. 


```{r}
#| label: Data Acquisition
load_netflix_data <- function(){

  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event) |>
    
  rename(title = Title,
         runtime = 'Runtime',
         views = 'Views',
         hours_viewed = 'Hours Viewed',
         release_date = 'Release Date',
         available_globally = 'Available Globally?')
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```
  

## 3. Fixing Facts

Using `mutate()` function, need to fix the 'year' and 'available_globally' columns to covert the data types for both columns.           
      
```{r}
#| label: Data Facts
NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
    mutate(
      year = as.integer(year),
      available_globally = available_globally == 'Yes')
```

##4. Exploratory Data Analysis
To ensure Data consistency across your dataset, perform few validation checks using the below functions to get a summary of each column **metadata** and the first few observations.

```{r}
#| label: Initial Summary
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```
After performing glimpse() function, Analysts can also view summary statistics for each column using summary(). This helps to make **quick business ops** decisions in real time.
```{r}
#| label: Structure
summary(NETFLIX_DATA)
```
Another useful function to get a *bit more structured* summary of the dataset and additional KPIs *eg. percentile* and little histograms is using the **skim()** from the ##skimr library.

```{r}
#| label: Statistics
library(skimr)
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```
## USP
By performing the above functions on our Netflix viewership dataset, analysts can find out the viewers engagement time on the platform by considering operational metrics like average for views, hours_viewed and runtime.

## 5. Exploratory Questions
* What date range is covered by this data set?
We can compute the Date range for the dataset by looking at the *period_start* and *period_end* column.

```{r}
#| label: Data Dates
range(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start, NETFLIX_DATA$period_end, na.rm = TRUE)
```
* How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?
To compute the No. titles (for multiple seasons and sequels), we summarise the title column across all the periods.
```{r}
#| label: Netflix Contents
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(uniq_titles = n_distinct(title))

```
* How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the Bridgerton universe?
For *Bridgerton* Universe total view-time, we simply filtered the title and summarise the total watch_time across all the periods.

```{r}
#| label: Bridgerton Universe
bridgerton_univ <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, 'Bridgerton')) |>
  summarise(total_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
bridgerton_univ
```

* How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things?
To compute the watch-time across the 5 seasons of Stranger Things (only season episodes), we filtered out all the auxiliary associations of the title. 

```{r}
#| label: Strangers
stranger_things_summary <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, 'Stranger Things')) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, 'Beyond|Tales from|Fireplace' )) |>
  summarise(total_hrs = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE))

stranger_things_summary

```
* What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?
To compute the share for watch-hours spent on top ten titles for the 1st half of 2026, we divided the content watch-time with the total hours viewed for **2026H1**.

```{r}
#| label: Top 10 Slicers
library(scales)
h1_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == '2026H1') |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10) |>
  mutate(pcent = percent(hours_viewed/ sum(hours_viewed))) |>
  select(title, hours_viewed, pcent) 

h1_2026

```
## 6. Tabular Analysis

* What was the top title (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?
To compute the Top Title for every period and its share in total watch-time, we calculated the fraction by dividing the content watch_time with the total hours viewed for every period.

```{r}
#| label: Top Title
top_title_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(total_viewtime = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1) |>
  mutate(frac_total = hours_viewed/ total_viewtime,
         share = percent(frac_total, accuracy = 0.01)) |>
  select(period, title, total_viewtime, frac_total, share)
  

top_title_period
```

* How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions?
To compute the Netflix catalog changes over time, we calculated No. of content published within each period and the period runtime across all the titles for every period.

```{r}
#| label: Catalog Growth
catalog_growth <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(n_titles = n_distinct(title),
            total_runtime = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE)/ 60,
            avg_runtime = mean(runtime, na.rm = TRUE),
            total_watchtime = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(period) |>
  mutate(
    title_growth = percent((n_titles - lag(n_titles)) / lag(n_titles), accuracy = 0.1),
    runtime_growth = percent((total_runtime - lag(total_runtime)) / lag(total_runtime), accuracy = 0.1)

  )

catalog_growth
```

* Which titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back on as ‘comfort food’, e.g., re-runs of Friends. 

A metric like **minimum hours viewed** or **median hours viewed** across periods would be ideal to compute the consistency over periods.

```{r}
#| label: Consistent Titles
total_periods <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

consistent_staples <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    no._periods = n_distinct(period),
    total_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_hours = min(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    filter(no._periods == total_periods) |>
    slice_max(min_hours, n = 15) |>
    mutate(
      cv_stability = percent(sd_hours/ mean_hours, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  
consistent_staples |>
  select(title, no._periods, total_hours, min_hours, median_hours, cv_stability)

consistent_staples

```

* Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?

To solve the query for watch time spent on *TV Shows* and *Movies* within each period. We start by defining and classifying *TV Shows* and *Movies* i.e. content having more than runtime of 210 minutes (3.5 hours) is a TV show and titles with runtime between 40 and 210 minutes is a *Movie*.  

```{r}
#| label: Shows vs Movies
tv_pattern <- regex(
  '\\b(Season|Series|Part|Volume|Vol\\.|Chapter|Episode|Episodes|Limited Series|Miniseries|Collection)\\b', ignore_case = TRUE
)

class_netflix <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = case_when(
      str_detect(title, tv_pattern) ~ "TV Show",
      runtime > 210 ~ "TV Show",
      runtime >= 40 & runtime <= 210 ~ "Movie",
      runtime > 180 ~ "TV Show",
      TRUE ~ "Movie"
    )
  )
content_type_summary <- class_netflix |>
  summarise(
    viewed_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    type_runtime = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
    n_titles = n_distinct(title),
    .by = c(period, content_type)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    period_total_runtime = sum(viewed_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    watch_pattern = viewed_hours / period_total_runtime,
    share = percent(watch_pattern, accuracy = 0.1),
    .by = period
  ) |>
  arrange(period, content_type)

content_type_summary


```

**How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?**

By computing Average Viewed hours `average_hours` for *Live Events* and *Pre taped content*, certainly *Pre taped content * draw more viewership in average watch-time than that of Taped content.Also, we can observe same pattern while comparing the Top_tier segment of both the classes.

```{r}
#| label: Live Event vs Originals
average_comp <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    n_titles = n(),
    average_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    medi_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_views = mean(views, na.rm = TRUE),
    medi_views = median(views, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = live_event
  ) |>
  mutate(
    formatt = if_else(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre-taped content"),
    across(c(average_hours, medi_hours, average_views, medi_views), comma)
  ) |>
  select(formatt, n_titles, average_hours, medi_hours, average_views, medi_views)

average_comp


top_tier_comp <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    p90_hours = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    p95_hours = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_hours = max(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_views = max(views, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = live_event
  ) |>
  mutate(
    frmt = if_else(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre taped content"),
    across(where(is.numeric), comma)
  ) |>
  select(frmt, p90_hours, p95_hours, max_hours, max_views)

top_tier_comp


```

## Corporate Strategy Memo

**To:** Netflix Executive Leadership
**FROM:** Dhruv Rajpal (Business Analyst)
**SUBJECT:** Data-Driven Strategic Directives for Original Content (2027 & Onward)

## Executive Summary

Analysis of semi-annual **What We Watched engagement** data across the **2023–2026** reporting cycles reveals structural insights into subscriber viewing patterns. Total platform consumption has leveled at roughly 90 to 95 billion hours per half-year, indicating that future growth must focus on capital retention efficiency and catalog monetization rather than **raw volume expansion**.

To maximize ROI on 2027 production budgets, I recommend allocating development capital around three core data realities:
1. The Structural Primacy of Multi-Episode TV Series over standalone feature films.

2. The Enduring Dominance of the Catalog Long-Tail over top-tier tentpoles.

3. The High-Efficiency "Eventization" of Live Shows/ Games to solve franchise decay.

4. Enrichment in UI/ UX for **Netflix Games** and remote controller connectivity.

5. Investment on better recommendation engines with Machine Learning Algorithms.

## Key Empirical Findings


1. Series vs. Feature Films: Hours vs. Reach

Across consistent reporting periods, TV Shows and OTT Series captures approximately 72% of total viewing hours, while feature films account for only 28% (e.g., 67.2B hours vs. 26.2B hours in 2023H1).

The Aggregate Run-time Advantage: A feature film offers 90 to 120 minutes of engagement per converted subscriber, whereas a standard 8-to-10 episode series demands average 300- 400 minutes of watch time.

Subscriber Value Retention: Standalone feature films frequently top initial weekly view counts, but episodic series drive repeat weekly sessions and minimize subscriber churn through multi-week sustained watch time.

2. Concentration Dynamics: The Top 10 vs. The Catalog Long-Tail

Despite heavy marketing investments in premier intellectual property, viewership remains distributed across a vast library:

  Title Ceiling: The single most-watched title in any 6-month period never captures more than 0.62% to 0.87% of     total viewing time (e.g., The Night Agent: S1 captured 812.1M hours, or 0.87% in 2023H1; Fool Me Once captured     583.0M hours, or 0.62% in 2024H1).

Top 10 Aggregate Share: In any single half-year cycle (such as 2026H1), the Top 10 titles collectively generate between 2.8% and 3.4% of total hours viewed. Over 96% of all platform consumption occurs across the remaining catalog long-tail and established comfort-viewing staples (Suits, Gilmore Girls, Cocomelon).

3. Live Broadcasts vs. Pre-Taped Originals

Live events (e.g., marquee roasts, sports exhibitions, comedy specials) account for fewer than 0.2% of all distinct catalog entries, yet they deliver distinct structural benefits:

Elevated Floor: Because live events are curated tentpoles, the average live event generates over 2.8× the mean viewership hours of the median pre-taped catalog release.
    
Peak Volume Trade-off: Top-tier live events peak between 20M and 65M hours, compared to 500M+ hours for premier episodic dramas like Bridgerton or Stranger Things. Live events drive acute sign-up bursts and cultural buzz, while pre-taped series build sustained, multi-year asset value

```{r}
#| label: Strategic portfolio
#| echo: false

#| label: Strategic-portfolio
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: Netflix Viewing Dynamics: Format Dominance vs. Platform Concentration
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-width: 11

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)

df_format <- data.frame(
  format = c("TV Series", "Feature Films"),
  share = c(0.72, 0.28)
)

p_format <- ggplot(df_format, aes(x = reorder(format, -share), y = share, fill = format)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)), vjust = -0.6, fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 0.85), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TV Series" = "#E50914", "Feature Films" = "#221F1F")) +
  labs(
    title = "A. Watch Time by Content Format",
    subtitle = "Episodic series~2.6x the cumulative watch time of movies",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of Total Platform Hours"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", size = 10),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

df_concentration <- data.frame(
  tier = factor(c("Catalog Long-Tail\n(Rank 11+)", "Top 10\nTentpoles"), 
                levels = c("Catalog Long-Tail\n(Rank 11+)", "Top 10\nTentpoles")),
  share = c(0.97, 0.03)
)

p_concentration <- ggplot(df_concentration, aes(x = tier, y = share, fill = tier)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)), vjust = -0.6, fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1.08), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Catalog Long-Tail\n(Rank 11+)" = "#221F1F", "Top 10\nTentpoles" = "#E50914")) +
  labs(
    title = "B. Viewership Concentration",
    subtitle = "97% of watch time is dispersed across the broader catalog",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of Total Platform Hours"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", size = 10),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

p_format + p_concentration
```

## Strategic Recommendations for 2027 and Beyond

Re balance the Slate Toward Returnable, Multi-Season TV (70/30 Budget Split):

Re-allocate film acquisition budgets toward developing recurring multi-season mid-budget procedural dramas and light comedies. Given that television generates ~72% of platform watch time, standalone $150M+ action films provide limited long-term retention compared to an established episodic universe.

**De-escalate Megahit Spending; Invest in Catalog Anchors:**

Because the Top 10 accounts for ~3% of platform hours, no individual mega-budget release can sustain user engagement alone. Redirect development funds toward acquiring and commissioning multi-year "comfort food" series (such as unscripted documentaries, workplace dromedaries, and kids/family animation) that maintain viewership floors above 15M hours across every reporting window.

**Deploy Live Events Strategically as Churn Breakers, Not Runtime Engines:**

Treat live sports, comedy specials, and reunions as customer-acquisition spikes rather than total watch-time drivers. Schedule live broadcasts strategically at the beginning of billing cycles to precede major season releases of high-engagement scripted dramas.

## Conclusion

Our competitive advantage in 2027 will not come from outspending rivals on high-risk, single-weekend blockbusters. By leveraging OTT series for baseline engagement and deploying high-impact live events for subscriber acquisition, Netflix can expand operating margins while reinforcing viewer retention.
